gloss: The lowest range of musical sound.
examples: Turn the *bass* down — the whole building can hear it.
You could feel the *bass* through the floor.
This mix has too much *bass* and no melody.
contrast: Spelled like *bass* /bæs/, the fish — a different word entirely. The fish has a zero plural (*two bass*); this one is regular (*two basses*).

gloss: A curved piece of wood strung tight, used to shoot arrows.
examples: He drew the *bow* back and let the arrow go.
Both *bows* were locked in the case.
She has shot a *bow* since she was ten.
contrast: Spelled like *bow* /baʊ/, the front of a ship, but said BOH to rhyme with *go* — a different word. The ribbon *bow* on a gift is this one.

gloss: The front end of a ship or boat.
examples: Waves broke over the *bow* all afternoon.
She stood at the *bow* watching for whales.
The *bows* of the old fishing boats were painted blue.
contrast: Spelled like *bow* /boʊ/, a knot or the weapon that shoots arrows, but said BOW to rhyme with *cow* — a different word. Bending forward to an audience — *take a bow* — is this one too.

gloss: A heavy, soft, gray metal that is poisonous to people.
examples: The inspector found *lead* in the old paint.
*Lead* feels much heavier than it looks.
They test the water for *lead* twice a year.
contrast: Spelled like *lead* /liːd/, the front position in a race, but said LED, exactly like *led* — a different word.

gloss: The front position in a race, game, or contest.
examples: She held the *lead* for three laps.
The home team gave up a ten-point *lead*.
Small *leads* disappear fast in this league.
contrast: Spelled like *lead* /lɛd/, the gray metal, but said LEED to rhyme with *need* — a different word. A dog's *lead* and the starring role are this one too.

gloss: A drop of the liquid that runs from the eye when you cry.
examples: A *tear* ran down his cheek before he could stop it.
She brushed away a *tear* and kept reading.
The whole ending had us in *tears*.
contrast: Spelled like *tear* /tɛr/, a rip in cloth, but said TEER to rhyme with *here* — a different word.

gloss: A hole made by pulling cloth or paper apart.
examples: There's a *tear* in the knee of my jeans.
He taped the *tear* in the map back together.
Two small *tears* in the seam turned into one big one.
contrast: Spelled like *tear* /tɪr/, a drop from the eye, but said TAIR to rhyme with *air* — a different word.

gloss: What is inside something, especially the text, video, or material it holds.
examples: The channel posts new *content* every Friday.
Check the sugar *content* on the label.
Most of the *content* on that site is copied.
contrast: Spelled like *content* /kənˈtɛnt/, a feeling of quiet satisfaction, but stressed on the first syllable — a different word.

gloss: A calm feeling of being satisfied with what you have.
examples: She read on the porch to her heart's *content*.
The kids ate ice cream to their heart's *content*.
There was a look of quiet *content* on his face.
contrast: Spelled like *content* /ˈkɑːntɛnt/, the material inside something, but stressed on the second syllable — a different word. Heard most often in *to one's heart's content*.

gloss: A large dry region with very little rain and almost no plants.
examples: Nights in the *desert* get surprisingly cold.
They crossed the *desert* before sunrise.
Several of the world's *deserts* are spreading.
contrast: Spelled like *desert* /dɪˈzɜːrt/, what a person deserves, but stressed on the first syllable — a different word.

gloss: What a person deserves, whether reward or punishment.
examples: The swindler finally got his just *deserts*.
Everyone in that story gets their just *deserts*.
The judge said the sentence was no more than his just *deserts*.
contrast: Spelled like *desert* /ˈdɛzərt/, the dry land, but stressed on the second syllable, like *dessert* — a different word. Almost always plural, in *just deserts*.

gloss: An informal short word for a graduate of a school or a former member of a group.
examples: She's an *alum* of the same high school as my brother.
The firm hires a lot of *alums* from that program.
Two *alums* came back to coach the team.
contrast: Spelled like *alum* /ˈæləm/, the chemical, but stressed on the second syllable — a different word.

gloss: A white powdery chemical used in pickling and to stop small cuts from bleeding.
examples: A little *alum* keeps the pickles crisp.
He touched *alum* to the nick from shaving.
The recipe calls for a teaspoon of *alum*.
contrast: Spelled like *alum* /əˈlʌm/, a graduate, but said AL-uhm with the stress up front — a different word.

gloss: A soft leather cloth used to dry glass and car paint without streaks.
examples: Dry the car with a *chamois* so it doesn't spot.
He kept a damp *chamois* in a bucket by the hose.
Good *chamois* cost more than a pack of towels.
contrast: Spelled like *chamois* /ʃæmˈwɑː/, the mountain animal, but said SHAM-ee — a different word. The plural is spelled the same.

gloss: A small goat-antelope that lives high in the mountains of Europe.
examples: A *chamois* can climb almost vertical rock.
We spotted two *chamois* on the ridge above the trail.
The soft leather was originally made from *chamois*.
contrast: Spelled like *chamois* /ˈʃæmi/, the polishing cloth, but said sham-WAH — a different word. The plural is spelled the same.

gloss: A short book that teaches the basics of a subject.
examples: The article is a good *primer* on how tariffs work.
She wrote a *primer* for first-time landlords.
Children once learned to read from *primers*.
contrast: Spelled like *primer* /ˈpraɪmər/, the base coat of paint, but said PRIM-ur in American English — a different word.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A first coat of paint that seals a surface so the color coat will stick.
examples: Roll on *primer* before you paint the walls.
The stain bled through two coats of *primer*.
Tinted *primers* can save you a coat of paint.
contrast: Spelled like *primer* /ˈprɪmər/, the beginner's book, but said PRY-mur — a different word.

gloss: An underground pipe that carries away waste water.
examples: The *sewer* backed up after the storm.
Crews are replacing century-old *sewers* downtown.
That smell is coming from the *sewer*.
contrast: Spelled like *sewer* /ˈsoʊər/, a person who sews, but said SOO-ur — a different word.

gloss: A person who sews.
examples: My grandmother was a fine *sewer*.
Experienced *sewers* can fix a hem in minutes.
You don't have to be an expert *sewer* to make a pillowcase.
contrast: Spelled like *sewer* /ˈsuːər/, the waste pipe, but said SOH-ur, from *sew* — a different word.

gloss: The benefit or purpose for which something is done.
examples: They stayed in town for the kids' *sake*.
For the *sake* of argument, say she's right.
Oh, for goodness' *sake*, just call her back.
contrast: Spelled like *sake* /ˈsɑːki/, the Japanese rice wine, but said SAYK, like *cake* — a different word.

gloss: A Japanese alcoholic drink brewed from rice.
examples: They warmed the *sake* and poured it into tiny cups.
He ordered cold *sake* with dinner.
The restaurant has a long *sake* list.
contrast: Spelled like *sake* /seɪk/, as in *for the sake of*, but said SAH-kee in two syllables — a different word.
